name: SS radio message to Lippert
date: 9 February 1944 (per a commenter's reading of the form's 'Tag/Monat' field, 'Mi' = Mittwoch/Wednesday, and 9 Feb 1944 was a Wednesday)
ciphertext: MASS=QRLZ / H9/OSLY / ALAP=DETL / 27163:KSSY / J1=EFLS / KOMM P4SX (ciphers/ss-radio-lippert-1944/ciphertext.txt, one blind pass off images/SS-Code.jpg, 25 Sept 2026, LANE B3 worker bSSR)
alphabet: 45 symbols total (37 letters, 8 digits): 18 distinct letters (A D E F H J K L M O P Q R S T X Y Z), 7 distinct digits (1,2,3,4,6,7,9); five of six lines divided internally by an equal sign, a slash or a colon (line 6, KOMM P4SX, has no separator character) -- 'None of the WW2 encryption methods I know produces ciphertexts that look like this' (Schmeh)

constraints.separators: five of six lines divided by =, / or :
constraints.sender: signature reads an SS-Untersturmführer (lieutenant) whose name might have been 'Klein or similar' per Schmeh; a rank/office stamp accompanies the signature
constraints.receiver: addressed to an SS-Standartenführer (colonel-equivalent) named Lippert
constraints.owner: original owned by US professor Nick Gessler (Duke University), photographed by Schmeh at a crypto-history conference
constraints.partial_decrypts_from_comments: blog readers proposed partial glosses of some groups without a full solve, none verified: ALAP = a village in Hungary (commenter Thomas); KSSY claimed = Budapest (commenter Oliver Helweg, disputed by Thomas -- no supporting source found); MASS = 'Marschbefehl für die SS' (march order); QRLZ = 'Vereinigung mit' (union/joining with); H9 = 9. SS-Panzer-Division 'Hohenstaufen'; J1 possibly 1. Panzerdivision; KOMM = 'Kommandant' or 'Kommando' (disputed among commenters); P4SX possibly Generaloberst Hube -- all per commenter Michaela Ellguth's 8-9 Aug 2017 reading, explicitly speculative, not a cryptanalytic solution, and contested by other commenters below
constraints.authenticity_dispute: a long comment thread (comments 9-27, Aug 2017) argues the document is a forgery: the rank-stamp eagle faces the wrong direction for a genuine Reichsadler stamp of the period, 'Lublin' is misspelled on the stamp ('Cztl.' for 'Kztl.'), Fraktur-s usage is inconsistent, the sender's unit (10. SS-Panzer-Division, stationed in France Feb 1944) does not match the stamp's origin (Lublin concentration camp, eastern Poland), rank abbreviations are non-standard (StdF instead of Staf; capital F instead of lowercase f), and a near-identical forged 'Funkspruch' was later sold on eBay by a named dealer (comment 28, 31 May 2021) -- UNSOLVED-SURVEY.md's row already records 'Bourdeau: probable forgery (typography, rank abbreviations)', consistent with this thread
constraints.unusual_form: Schmeh: none of the WW2 encryption methods he knows produce ciphertexts with this internal =, /, : punctuation -- worth comparing against the standard German WW2 Wehrmacht/SS Spruchformular layout (a successor form existed from May 1941, per commenter Thomas, cryptomuseum.com/crypto/enigma/forms) once transcribed, since the punctuation may mark form fields (addressee/date/serial) rather than cipher structure

cheap_tests_in_order: 1. Fetch SS-Code.jpg (scienceblogs.de, already on disk as sources/schmeh/posts/25-ss-radio.html's embedded link; direct image not yet saved) and transcribe the six lines blind, recording the =, /, : separator positions exactly. Cost $1-2, Sonnet.

2. Once transcribed, compare the form's field layout (date, addressee, serial number fields implied by the punctuation) against the WW2 Wehrmacht Spruchformular and its May-1941 successor (cryptomuseum.com/crypto/enigma/forms, named by a commenter) to separate plaintext form-fields from actual cipher groups before attempting any language judge. Cost $1.

3. If a cipher-group segment is isolated, run it against German with a matched control (synthetic German plaintext of the same N, same solver) -- but treat the authenticity dispute (constraints.authenticity_dispute) as a live possibility that no amount of cryptanalysis resolves: a forged Funkspruch may encode nothing at all. Cost $2-3.
matched_control: run 25 Sept 2026: German-prose control (tools/data/de20, era-matched 1880-1940, N=37 letters, 5 seeds x 200 draws) mean IC 0.0725 [0.0465,0.1066]; uniform-random control (K=18, N=37, 5 seeds x 200 draws) mean IC 0.0554 [0.0420,0.0751]

cheap_test_done.method: fetched images/SS-Code.jpg (scienceblogs.de), single blind transcription pass, no subagent; computed letter-only index of coincidence (specs/cheap-tests/ss-radio-lippert-1944/ic_test.py) against a German-prose control (tools/data/de20, same N) and a uniform-random control (same K), both at 5 seeds x 200 draws
cheap_test_done.verdict: inconclusive -- target IC falls inside both 95% ranges; N=37 letters split across six short code-like groups is too little text for IC to discriminate at all, not a control-backed negative either way

judge.note: letters_min/max is a rough guess pending transcription (six short lines with internal punctuation, no letter count known yet); narrow once real counts exist

value: low: a well-documented, multi-commenter authenticity dispute (forged rank stamp, misspelled Lublin, mismatched unit/location, a near-identical item later sold as a forgery on eBay) makes this more likely a collectible fake than a real wartime message -- any cryptanalytic campaign should be preceded by, not substitute for, resolving the forgery question, and even a fluent-looking German decode would not settle authenticity
